entries.note: “Peak bubble” is an emphatic characterization without a testable peak criterion.

entries.test: OpenAI's publicly reported cash and available financial resources at publication would establish whether it had $300 billion.
entries.note: This appears in the passage introduced by “I quote the first bit,” rather than in Marcus's own voice.

entries.test: OpenAI's publicly reported financial resources at publication would show whether its available funds were substantially below $300 billion.
entries.note: This is part of the explicitly introduced quotation.

entries.test: Public reporting or disclosures of OpenAI's contemporaneous financial projections would establish whether they placed its first profitable year in 2030.
entries.note: This is within the introduced quotation. The core claim concerns what a projection said, not whether profitability actually arrives in 2030.

entries.test: OpenAI's public statements about GPT-5 and independent evaluations of its released capabilities would test the claimed AGI expectation and whether the product met it.
entries.note: Public statements can establish the “claimed” alternative without establishing a private belief.

entries.test: Oracle's contemporaneous hardware capacity, contract requirements, cash holdings, and chip acquisition costs would establish whether it lacked both the required chips and the cash to purchase them.
entries.note: “The contracts” refers to the deal under discussion; the normalization broadens this to Oracle's AI cloud contracts generally.
Being astounded by collection expresses strong doubt, not a firm prediction that collection will fail.

The main conclusion judges the valuation's rationality; its numerical premises are separately checkable. The normalization also strengthens “seems more bonkers than most” into an unqualified judgment.

entries.test: The referenced chart's two rightmost revenue projections and Oracle's contemporaneous market capitalization increase would settle the comparison.
entries.note: The two rightmost projected bars are not necessarily the next two forecast periods.
The comparison depends on what the companies are “likely ever” to deliver in the future.
“Peak musical chairs” is a metaphor without a testable threshold.
The prediction specifies neither the adverse outcome nor who experiences it, leaving no shared test for “not going to be pretty.”
